description.narrative:
In just two years, the Climate Justice Camp (CJC) has grown into the largest global platform of its kind, bringing together hundreds of organizers, activists, advocates, and community leaders working at the intersection of climate and social justice. This unique space facilitates members of diverse movements in the Global South to meet face-to-face; and build knowledge, strategies, capacity, community, and networks that are taken back to communities on the frontlines of climate change, resulting in real-world and long-term action. Over the period of a week, participants develop, take part in, and lead workshops and events focused on a series of thematic strands with concrete objectives. Participants are carefully selected to represent a broad range of backgrounds and sectors, including climate justice, conservation, social justice, human rights, humanitarian, women’s rights <(>&<)> feminism, Indigenous rights and LGBTQIA+ issues. In 2022, the first CJC in Tunisia gathered 350 organizers from 65 countries. The following year, the 2023 camp held in Lebanon hosted 450 leaders from nearly 100 nations. These camps involved support from more than 200 organizations, attractedover 10,000 applications, and have led to an active community of 500+ members who remain in touch and continue to collaborate. The CJC is gaining visibility globally each year, and has been the subject of over 70 media reports, including coverage by top-tier outlets like The Guardian, the BBC, EFE News Agency, Infobae, ABC, Al Hurra, Dubai TV, and Al Mayadeen. On digital platforms, posts under the Climate Justice Camp hashtags have garnered over 113,000 interactions, and videos over 1,717,041 views. The Climate Justice Camp was mentioned in over 700 posts, reaching a potential audience of over 12 million people. We also had a range of social media influencers in attendance, who posted about the camp to their collective audiences of hundreds of thousands of people; the camp was featured on accounts including Feminist, Earthly Education, Intersectional Environmentalist, and Atmos. ● Recap from Tunisia ● Recap from Lebanon Given the tremendous interest, energy, and support emanating from young organizers in Sub-Saharan Africa, the Climate Justice Camp has made the strategic decision to host its third edition in Arusha, Tanzania at the MS Training Center for Development Cooperation from the 8th-12th October 2024. The impact of the previous editions in Tunisia and Lebanon has been transformative, driving real-world and long-term action at local, regional, and international levels that present a significant opportunity to channel themomentum and collaborative spirit into Sub-Saharan Africa.
Climate Justice Camp Objectives The Climate Justice Camp serves as a dynamic hub for building meaningful relationships, fostering networks, and forging alliances among groups dedicated to climate justice, social justice, and youth engagement. Additionally, the CJC provides a crucial opportunity for youth advocates to strategically plan and enhance their engagement, maximizing their influence and effectiveness at following UNFCCC COPs. This inclusive space brings together civil society actors, local community advocates, and passionate organizers to create impactful connections, promote collaboration, and unite efforts to deliver strategic impact. 1. Co-creation of cross-border and cross-issue strategies: a. Strategic development: In this collaborative space, grassroots groups co-create strategies, tactics, narratives, and symbols to build cross-border solidarity and design impactful campaigns. b. Mobilization plans and advocacy for systemic change: The CJC program prominently features discussions on Climate Finance, Adaptation, and Just Transition. 2. Building relationships, networks and alliances a. Facilitating connection through storytelling sessions: The CJC provides a platform for organizers and groups to engage in storytelling sessions, where participants can share and listen to local stories, lessons learned, and best practices. b. Networking and community building for lasting connections: Encouraging networking and community building, the CJC enables groups to connect across issues, geographies, and demographics. c. Cross-border solidarity in inclusive spaces: The camp provides open, safe, and inclusive spaces for local organizers and advocates to discuss their specific contexts and community needs. 3. Building capacity and communities of practice: By bringing people together from across the region, the CJC creates opportunities for a diverse range of training, workshops, and capacity development initiatives. Participants gain access to a myriad of sessions offered by partners, the coordination team, and fellow participants. Additionally, thecamp aims to establish regional communities of practice, ensuring that shared learnings and best practices continue to be connected and utilized beyond the camp.

participating-org.narrative:
Established in 2018, Greenpeace MENA is the newest organization of the Greenpeace network.
Greenpeace MENA has a regional operation in the Middle East and North Africa with an ongoing continuous presence in several countries in the region.
Greenpeace MENA offers solutions to the major environmental problems in the Middle East and North African region, notably the climate emergency. We work hand in hand with diverse regional and national stakeholders, focusing our work where we have expertise and experience and where we can make the greatest impact and contribution.
Greenpeace MENA seeks to promote a greener, more sustainable and more equitable future for everyone. We believe that a better world is not only possible, but is already happening.
